articles.headline: Spanish prime minister calls meeting over ‘migration emergency’ as thousands surge into Canary Islands
keyFacts: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an emergency meeting after over 5,500 migrants arrived in the Canary Islands over one week.
Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo demanded immediate state resources and action to prevent local public services from falling short.
Spanish immigration officials and Canary Islands leaders will meet on Tuesday to discuss emergency responses and resource allocation.
body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is calling a meeting to address the developing “emergency” on the Canary Islands, which have become the latest point of failure in the country’s immigration framework.

The Canary Islands, Spain’s southernmost territory that sits off the northwest coast of Africa, have recently experienced a massive surge in illegal immigration. Over the past week, over 50 boats reportedly carrying more than 5,500 migrants arrived at the islands— overwhelming public services and creating what officials call a “migration emergency.”

“The Canary Islands have been calling for cooperation, coordination and resources for weeks to prevent what we are seeing today on El Hierro,” Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said Monday ahead of the meeting with Sanchez. “We cannot allow resources to fall short or the island to end up being turned into a massive detention center. Neither one nor the other.”
Migrants disembark at the port of “La Estaca” in Valverde at El Hierro, Canary Islands, Spain, Aug. 26, 2024. (Maria Ximena/AP Photo, file)

“We demand concrete commitments, resources and immediate action,” he continued. “El Hierro and the Canary Islands deserve a response from the State that matches the solidarity, dignity and responsibility this land has demonstrated.”

The Tuesday meeting will convene officials of the Interministerial Commission on Immigration. The Canary Islands will be represented by Clavijo and Alpidio Armas — the president of El Hierro, the largest island in the territory.

Over the last five weeks, approximately 8,000 migrants are believed to have entered the Canary Islands illegally. Many more have perished on the treacherous journey by boat from countries including Senegal, Gambia, Guinea, and Nigeria.

At least 39 victims were killed in a shipwreck discovered over the weekend off the coast of Senegal. The boat had been broken apart off the coast of Senegal at an unknown point, and bodies were found in an advanced state of decomposition.
Armas said his island is one of the preeminent points of entry for West African migrants to enter the European Union illegally.
“This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions,” he said in a Saturday interview with Spanish media.
The Canary Islands are only the latest to suffer from illegal migrants flooding into Spanish overseas territories.

Earlier this year, the autonomous region of Ceuta experienced a total collapse of border security as thousands of Moroccans similarly surged over walls and swam across bodies of water. An estimated 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta, a city-state with only 84,000 legitimate residents.

The overload created chaos in public life as crime spiked, schools were disrupted, hospitals were overburdened, and squatters set up large encampments on beaches and in city centers. The government claimed 15,000 illegal migrants remained in Ceuta at the time of the press conference.
In late October, Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas lamented at a press conference that his region “has not returned to normal almost three months later.”

“No one has yet been returned through administrative resolution, and all those who have left have done so through voluntary returns or for committing crimes — so it seems that the government’s strategy is for this to collapse under its own weight,” Vivas lamented.

Migrants queue at a public service office to obtain paperwork needed to apply for Spain’s immigration amnesty in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat near Barcelona, Spain, on April 21, 2026. (Emilio Morenatti/AP Photo, file)

“The situation is extraordinarily far from normal, and every day that passes it gets worse because our capacity to resist is weakening, and it seems we’re at a dead end,” he continued. “No one can stand this injustice.”
Sanchez rolled out a program in April giving illegal immigrants inside Spain a pathway to legal residency.
SPANISH PRIME MINISTER PROMISES TO RELEASE ALL FILES ON CEUTA INVASION AS THOUSANDS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS REMAIN IN ENCLAVE
Applicants who have lived in the country for at least five months and have no criminal record may apply for the program and renew their legal status on an annual basis.
The prime minister and his government said prior to the rollout that they expected 500,000 illegal residents to benefit from the program, but over 1 million individuals applied.

articles.headline: Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers.
keyFacts: Researchers estimate the U.S. will need 625,000 to 1.3 million additional direct care workers by 2036 as the population ages.
Policy experts say bringing in immigrant caregivers is necessary because the U.S.-born workforce cannot meet the growing direct care demand.
Bipartisan lawmakers have introduced caregiving visa proposals after President Donald Trump expressed openness to an immigration reform deal.
body: Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less debate among policymakers about how large America’s older population will be in a decade’s time, and how many of them are likely to need direct care for disabilities.

By 2036, as the baby boomers continue to retire, the US population 65 and older is expected to grow from 65.6 million to 77.5 million people, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The number of people 85 and older is also expected to nearly double in that time, from 6.8 million to 11.1 million.

The question of whether the United States will have enough direct care workers — an umbrella term that refers to home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants — looms large. These are workers, primarily women, who help older adults and people with disabilities bathe, dress, eat, take their medication, and generally get through a day, either in a nursing home or in someone’s own home. It’s a massive, often ignored workforce (the American Community Survey estimates there were 3.62 million of them in 2024) and it’s paid for largely by Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program that most people associate with coverage for impoverished Americans but which is actually the dominant payer for long-term care in this country.
Key takeaways
By 2036 the US will need 625,000 to 1.3 million more direct care workers, and policymakers across the aisle agree the demand is real and coming.

Three bipartisan-friendly proposals — the Dignity Act, the Careworker Visa Act, and a Brookings caregiving visa — would bring in immigrant caregivers with built-in protections learned from past programs.

With around 40 cosponsors from both parties and Problem Solvers Caucus backing, the Dignity Act has more bipartisan traction than most immigration bills in years. Trump has also expressed new openness to immigration reform.

Depending on which researcher you ask, the US will need somewhere between 625,000 and 1.3 million additional direct care workers over the next decade to keep pace with the growing number of older and disabled Americans — and that’s just to maintain today’s level of care as the population ages, not to fix the shortage that already exists. If you’ve talked to anyone currently trying to coordinate long-term care, you probably already know the country is understaffed as it is.

To close the gap, policy experts say the United States should bring more immigrants into a sector that’s already about one-third immigrant , while also protecting the roughly 12 percent of current direct care workers who are noncitizens, some of them undocumented. PHI, a national nonprofit that researches and advocates for the direct care workforce, projects 9.6 million direct care job openings between 2025 and 2035, the bulk of which will come from existing workers changing fields, retiring, or otherwise leaving the workforce.
“We can’t do it with the current US-born workforce,” Amy Robins, the senior director of policy at PHI, told me. “We need to have mechanisms where people can come into this country and do this work.”

Immigration reform has felt politically impossible in Washington for years, but after the brutal defeat Republicans suffered in the midterms, there’s a suddenly a much stronger case that this corner of the fight is different. Days after the election, President Donald Trump gave an interview saying his deportation policy was “too tough” and he’d be open to some sort of immigration reform deal to protect workers. In September 2025, Sens. Kevin Cramer (R-ND) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) reintroduced a bill to recover green cards that went unused in earlier years and redirect them to nurses and doctors. Coordinating care for older adults is a problem that reaches families in every corner of the country, and even comfortable households wonder whether they can secure a dignified life for an aging parent, or, eventually, for themselves.

With family caregivers growing in number and nursing homes turning residents away because they can’t find staff, caregiving may be the one corner of immigration policy Congress is actually willing to fix.
A growing menu of options
Over the last year or so, three different proposals have emerged that suggest that caregiving is the immigration battle Washington is finally ready to fight.

In July 2025, Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) and Veronica Escobar (D-TX) introduced the Dignity Act , which pairs tougher border enforcement with legal status for undocumented immigrants who’ve been in the country since before 2021. It also offers permanent residency for Dreamers and a handful of green card reforms. Salazar herself has pitched the bill partly as a remedy for the same aging-population squeeze driving the caregiver shortage, and eldercare groups such as LeadingAge and the American Seniors Housing Association have thrown their support behind it .
The legislation rests on an idea at the center of the caregiving political fight, which is that immigration enforcement alone won’t get the US the labor it needs.

Since then, the Dignity Act has gathered around 40 cosponsors, split nearly down the middle between the parties, and this spring it won the endorsement of the Problem Solvers Caucus, a group of roughly 60 members whose mandate is passing legislation both sides can live with. Following Trump’s recent comments that he’d be open to an immigration deal, Salazar praised him on X, urging him to throw his weight behind the Dignity Act. “You can surpass Reagan’s legacy by delivering a historic immigration reform,” she posted. “This is your moment.”

There are other ideas on the table, too. Over the summer, Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-NM) introduced the Careworker Visa Act , a bill that would create a new temporary visa allowing up to 100,000 immigrants a year to work in childcare, eldercare, and home-based disability care. It would also let some immigrants already living in the US obtain work authorization through the program and give participating workers a pathway to permanent residency.

“We all know that immigrants are already taking on these jobs in large numbers,” Vasquez told me. “One of the conversations we’re having amongst the Democratic coalition is how to craft meaningful immigration-related legislation that can be bipartisan on a couple specific issues. And certainly this bill rises to the very top of that conversation.”

And the most recent entry came in September, from Tara Watson, an economist at the Brookings Institution. In a new caregiving visa proposal , she offers the idea of a visa open to immigrants with at least two years of direct care experience who want to come to the US to work as home health aides, personal care aides, or nursing assistants. It would start at 30,000 visas a year before rising to 65,000 after three years, and employers would have to pay above-market wages and provide health insurance.
Learning from what didn’t work

Neither of the two dedicated caregiving visa proposals is starting from scratch. In 1999, Congress created a visa for nurses to work in understaffed hospitals, but the process had such strict eligibility rules that fewer than 15 hospitals nationwide ever qualified to use it. And it was burdensome for qualifying workers, too: If a nurse ever wanted to switch their hospital, they had to start their visa certification process all over again. Over the course of a decade, barely a thousand visas were ever issued, and lawmakers let the program expire in 2009.

Other countries have gone the opposite direction. The UK made care workers eligible for its Health and Care Worker visa in 2022 , and the numbers took off almost immediately, with 106,000 visas granted in 2023 alone. But exploitation was rampant. Some contracts required workers to repay thousands of pounds to their employer if they left before their visa term was up — one worker’s contract demanded more than 11,000 British pounds — which made leaving a bad job financially impossible for people who’d often already gone into debt just to get the job in the first place. More than 43,000 workers were affected when their employers’ sponsor licenses were revoked amid widespread reports of exploitation. The UK ended overseas recruitment for care workers in 2025, though the broader Health and Care Worker visa remains in place.

Both experiments reflected the fact that workers often had no way out, no matter how poorly an employer behaved. Watson and Vasquez say they kept that front of mind when crafting their proposals, both of which allow workers to switch jobs rather than staying locked to whoever sponsored them.

“You really do see this tension — the more you try to make sure the workers are protected, the more onerous it becomes for the employers,” Watson told me. “You’re choosing between scale and some of those restrictions. I’m trying to hit somewhat of a middle ground.”
Vasquez pointed to the H-2A visa program for farmworkers, which he said has also had real, ongoing problems with employers abusing the system.

“Anytime that we are creating new programs for immigrant workers in which their job status depends on them achieving legal status, we should always be aware that there may be bad folks that are seeking to abuse that system,” he told me. “That’s going to require some thoughtful support for the Department of Labor for enforcement of laws just like this.”
States can’t fix this alone

These federal ideas build on top of a patchwork of state-level attempts to raise direct care wages in order to incentivize more people living here to enter and stay in the field. Yet for all the state mandates, bonuses, and training programs, care programs are usually among the first casualties when money gets tight. And even in states that have pulled off real wage increases, inflation has frequently swallowed those gains before they could do much to close the gap.

LeadingAge, which represents nonprofit nursing homes, assisted living communities, and home care agencies, says no single state’s budget can fix this. Linda Couch, the organization’s senior vice president of policy, says states are now facing significant cuts to their Medicaid funding under last year’s federal budget law, which will squeeze what providers can pay their staff.

“Federal policymakers hold a lot of the cards for systemic change to meet the needs of older adults,” Couch told me. “Without action to secure immigration reform and reverse Medicaid cuts, we’re putting access to aging services at risk for older adults across the country.”

LeadingAge’s members are already feeling this. Couch said one of its Massachusetts members, Hebrew SeniorLife, had to let go of nearly 40 Haitian workers this year after their Temporary Protected Status ended, some of whom had worked there for more than a decade. A Florida provider lost 10 workers from Cuba and Haiti after a humanitarian parole program shut down .

Congressional Republicans to date have primarily rallied around tax credits and retirement protections for the nation’s 63 million family caregivers . Robins of PHI, though, doesn’t see the two approaches as inherently at odds.

“There are way more family caregivers in this country than there are direct care workers, and that will always be true,” she told me. It’s a “yes, and” when it comes to supporting family caregivers, she said, and direct care workers are a “fundamental way that we support family caregivers who are taking on tremendous care responsibilities in our country right now.” A paid home health aide coming a few days a week, in other words, can be what lets a daughter or spouse keep working, or just get a full night’s sleep, while still caring for a parent at home.

The population who will need this care by 2036 is already here. It may not be much, but caregiving, as Watson said, is “low-hanging fruit, if there is any low-hanging fruit.” In an immigration debate this stuck, that counts for something.

articles.headline: Newly elected Dem's blistering GOP attacks emerge after she courted Republican voters: 'Lit on fire'
keyFacts: South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews' past social media posts criticizing Republicans and supporting transgender rights resurfaced following her recent election victory.
During her campaign, Andrews presented a moderate image, courted independent and Republican voters, and distanced herself from some of her earlier positions.
Republicans highlighted her past statements during the race, while her campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
body: South Carolina’s Democratic senator-elect has a history of trashing Republicans and advocating passionately for transgender rights on social media, with many of those posts reemerging after her victory earlier this month.

"The T in LGBTQ+ stands for TRANSGENDER," Annie Andrews, who is set to represent a state President Donald Trump won by roughly 18%, posted in 2023. "If you don’t support trans people, keep your cute pride post in your draft tweets, be better, and try again next year."
"Periodic reminder that I support trans kids because I am not an a--hole," she posted around the same time.

The posts stand in stark contrast to the more moderate image Andrews presented during her successful campaign against Republican Sen. Darline Graham, when she courted Republicans and independents in the deep-red state and distanced herself from some of her earlier positions on transgender issues.
MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA

Beyond transgender issues, where she later distanced herself from certain positions in a campaign ad, Andrews also made her disdain clear for the Republican Party before running for Senate — statements that clashed with the emphasis she placed on bipartisanship while on the campaign trail.

In August 2024, Andrews stated that the Republican Party "needs to be lit on fire & thrown in the dumpster & plunged into the deepest depths of the ocean never to be seen again," after some individuals on social media mocked Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s son.
SC DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS SHE WILL STAND UP TO HER PARTY AS GRAHAM TIES HER TO 'SOCIALIST DEMOCRATS'
"Herpes is forever," she said in another post. " JD Vance doesn’t have to be."

"Wow they let you out of the kitchen. Congrats," Andrews wrote in a post reacting to GOP Sen. Katie Britt talking about a White House visit, making a jab at Britt with a reference to women being confined to traditional homemaking roles.
While Andrews had strong words for Republicans before launching her Senate bid, she worked to appease them in the lead-up to Election Day.

At an October town hall billed as "Republicans and Independents for Annie," for instance, she said the campaign was for people more concerned about bills, rural hospitals and government integrity than party labels. She repeatedly stated that she intended to work across the aisle if elected and that her campaign was "not just for Democrats."
DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING

Andrews made scores of other posts expressing support for abortion access, drag queen story hours and increased restrictions on firearm ownership, among other issues. She reposted one post calling semi-automatic rifles "weapons of war," for instance.

"Republicans spent all their money trying to defeat Abdul and hired zero opposition researchers on Annie," independent journalist Zaid Jilani wrote on X, responding to one of Andrews’ pro-transgender resurfaced posts.
WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS
While some have criticized Republicans for not capitalizing on Andrews’ posts while on the campaign trail, the GOP did dredge old statements in an attempt to dissuade voters from backing her.

"Annie Andrews launched her political career fighting for her trans agenda … dozens of comments and tweets advocating for dudes in girls' sports, procedures on minors, and more," National Republican Senatorial Committee advisor Nathan Brand posted in October, responding to an ad released by Andrews disavowing biological men in women’s sports . "Now she is walking it ALL back."

Republicans leaned heavily into transgender issues, particularly banning sex change procedures for children and biological men from competing in women’s sports, during the 2026 electoral cycle . While the focus on such issues did not prevent the GOP from losing what are usually safe seats, a number of ballot measures rolling back transgender rights passed in liberal states.
The Andrews campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

articles.headline: Hollow Knight Silksong physical editions mention multiple "free content packs" incoming, and call Sea of Sorrow a "giant expansion"
keyFacts: Physical editions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are arriving on players' doorsteps after being scheduled for delivery starting 10th November.
A pack-in manual reveals that developer Team Cherry plans to release multiple free content packs and a giant expansion named Sea of Sorrow.
The manual describes the Sea of Sorrow expansion as coming soon and featuring a salt-stricken ocean, though no specific release date was provided.
body: More than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are finally arriving on players' doorsteps. It's the same brilliant and sometimes thrillingly cruel Metroidvania Eurogamer gave five stars to, except this time a pack-in booklet seemingly reveals the existence of multiple "free content packs" alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

Hollow Knight: Silksong's physical editions were originally set to be delivered from 10th November, but some early handovers have given us a peek inside the box. Redditor Me_975 posted pictures of their Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, and there's a few interesting tidbits tucked away - most notably in the manual's chapter on Content Packs.
"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

Developer Team Cherry confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support last year, but remained pretty tight-lipped about what exactly that would look like. The indie outfit then announced the nautically themed Sea of Sorrow expansion, though we now have proper confirmation there's more content packs still to come, which shouldn't be a huge shocker considering all the free post-launch love Hollow Knight (the first one) received.
Speaking of Sea of Sorrow, that's mentioned here too: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace."

Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - time's a-ticking, Team Cherry. Still no release date so far, but the booklet does say it's "Coming Soon." Of course, Team Cherry are quite infamous for working on games until they balloon wildly out of control. After all, Silksong was once upon a time intended to be a Hollow Knight DLC, but with games this detailed, I can't really complain about waiting a little extra.

If you are interested in owning Silksong physically, it comes with a big map of Pharloom and the rest of the booklet also includes some really lovely art seemingly ripped straight from the game, as well.

articles.headline: Dianna Russini returns to sports media after Vrabel photo scandal with NFL betting show
keyFacts: Dianna Russini is launching a weekly NFL betting show with BetUS called The Russini Report.
The new project follows her resignation from The Athletic after an investigation into her relationship with Mike Vrabel.
Russini told People magazine that the past six months were heartbreaking and described the experience as a nightmare.
body: Dianna Russini will return to sports media with a weekly one-hour show focused on the NFL backed by offshore sportsbook BetUS, she announced Monday.

The Russini Report will stream on BetUS TV’s website and X account, accompanied by a weekly analysis column. BetUS has described the program as a “live NFL betting show” that will run through the remainder of the season with game previews, matchup breakdowns and guest interviews.
The news comes seven months after Russini resigned from her role as the Athletic’s top NFL insider amid an internal investigation into her relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.

In April, the New York Post published photos of Russini and Vrabel at an Arizona resort, taken around the time of the NFL owners meetings in March. Some appeared to show the two embracing and holding hands. Russini and Vrabel, who are married to other people, said the interaction was platonic. Russini said the photos did not reflect that they were part of a larger group gathering, and Vrabel called any suggestion of impropriety “laughable”.
The New York Times-owned outlet began a review of Russini’s work after additional photos and reporting raised questions about the nature of her relationship with Vrabel. Russini resigned on 14 April.

The Athletic’s investigation, the findings of which were announced in September, did not find signs of bias in her coverage but said her relationship with Vrabel was in “clear violation” of the newsroom’s standards.
Russini, 43, joined the Athletic in 2023 after an eight-year stint at ESPN.

In comments to People magazine on Monday, Russini described the events of this spring as “heartbreaking”. She did not directly address any of the allegations involving Vrabel, who was not investigated by the NFL for his involvement.
“The best way to describe what the last six months were like for me is heartbreaking,” Russini said. “At the beginning of this, it was a nightmare.”

“The absolute best part of this situation has been the loyalty the NFL has shown me,” she added, referring to support from players, coaches and others around the league. “They checked in with me almost daily while I wasn’t working to make sure that I was staying connected to football, to check on me as a person and to just see how I was doing.”
She said her new show would include analysis on the NFL “along with a lot of my opinions”, describing that as “something I wasn’t really allowed to do before.”

“The way I’m going to approach stories is going to be very different now,” she told People. “I have an understanding and an empathy that I didn’t have before. I would do stories in the past at the best of my ability, and sometimes now I reflect on those, and I don’t know if I always thought about how much this would affect not just the player, but a team, an organization, the players’ families.”

articles.headline: Man Utd yet to make decision on Carrick's future
keyFacts: Manchester United's board has not yet made a final decision on Michael Carrick's future following a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa.
The team sits in 18th place in the table after recording their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.
Manchester United will travel to play Liverpool on November 22 in their first match after the international break.
body: - Published
Manchester United's board is yet to make a final decision on Michael Carrick's future.
The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.
The draw was Carrick's third match in charge since the board decided to give the 45-year-old more time to improve the side's form after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October.

The board felt Carrick - and the players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around, while the heirachy were also aware that November's two-week break would offer an opportunity to reassess the situation in a calmer manner.
They are determined to do exactly that, knowing the results - one win, one draw and one defeat - and performances United have delivered in the past three games offer a mixed view of Carrick's tenure.

Conceding eight goals, winning only once and dropping into the relegation zone are obvious negatives. However, it is also felt fighting back from two goals down three times over the past two games showed that the players remain behind Carrick.
United's heirachy explored the possibility of replacing Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth last month, with ex-Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann considered.

Carrick said after the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa that he would not step down, but chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will be influential in the decision whether to keep the former Middlesbrough boss.
United travel to arch rivals Liverpool on 22 November in their first match after the international break, with Carrick's side in 18th place in the Premier League.
With just one league win so far this term, it is United's lowest position having played 10 matches since the 1986-87 campaign.

Following the Anfield trip, five of United's next seven league opponents are in the bottom half of the league. This includes the four other sides currently in the bottom five, with meetings against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland, all at Old Trafford.
Whether Carrick keeps his job or not, United will continue to struggle unless they stop conceding goals with such regularity.
Only Crystal Palace and Ipswich have let in more than United's 19 league goals.
They have conceded 15 times in the past three matches in all competitions. Their only clean sheet this term came against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK in the Champions League.
'Carrick will be puzzled'

"All the Premier League teams, whether they play home or away against Manchester United, fancy their chances because you can open them up and score goals," former United assistant boss Rene Meulensteen told BBC Radio Five Live.

"No matter what combination you find it's just not good enough. I think Michael Carrick will be constantly puzzled as to what back four he can play because there's no certainty they can keep a clean sheet."
Full-back Diogo Dalot took the brunt of fan ire at Old Trafford on Sunday.
Huge cheers greeted his number being shown to confirm he was being replaced, which then turned to boos when he reached the dugout.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee, who suffered similar treatment when he was replaced after half an hour of a home defeat to Newcastle in December 2024, made a point of hugging Dalot as he made his way back to the bench.
Asked if it was time to take Dalot out of the firing line, Carrick urged caution.
"We've got to be careful with that," he said.

"I understand the frustration and I understand the disappointment of the supporters, I get it. We're all frustrated, we're all disappointed, and the players are as much as anyone, I guarantee you that.
"Diogo gives absolutely everything. He's played in different positions and played really well at times.
"He gives a penalty away. He knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better. He made a mistake. But I like what he brings to the team. He cares an awful lot and he's giving everything."

articles.headline: NYC DSA is so afraid of being too white it’s mulling an ‘anti-oppression’ task force to recruit minorities
keyFacts: Members of the New York City Democratic Socialists of America are considering a resolution to create an anti-oppression task force to recruit more minorities and working-class residents.
Queens Borough President Donovan Richards said he welcomed the move to diversify but stated the task force should not be run by white members.
Civil rights leader Rev. Kevin McCall stated the DSA needs to open up the process to black and Hispanic communities in the five boroughs.
body: Members of the city’s Democratic Socialists of America think their roster is too white — and are considering an “anti-oppression” task force to recruit minorities and actual working-class New Yorkers.

The New York City chapter of the uber-liberal group will consider a resolution stuffed with politically correct messaging at its convention on Saturday that would create a “Task Force to Promote Equitable Organizing Culture” and force its leaders to get diversity training.
“NYC-DSA aims to build the power of the socialist movement by growing our base among the multiracial, multigendered working class of our city,” the proposed resolution said.

“DSA has historically faced well-documented challenges recruiting and retaining people of color, and NYC-DSA’s racial makeup does not reflect the racial diversity of our city,” the proposal added, also referring to the proposed group as an “anti-oppression” task force.

The resolution, if approved, would also require extensive training for DSA leadership. A recent internal survey found 60% of the city DSA’s members identified as white while the Big Apple is 34% white, The Post previously reported. The city chapter claims more than 15,000 members.

“The chapter will create an Anti-Oppression Task Force supported by the Membership Committee, which will be responsible for supporting leadership and membership to dismantle oppressive systems and combat oppressive practices in the chapter,” the resolution said.

“It is incumbent on NYC-DSA’s leadership to proactively learn about oppressive systems and behaviors, how to dismantle and combat them within the organization, and how to construct an equitable culture that advances our goals of organizing the multiracial, multigendered working class; as well as supporting the full membership to learn about these topics and enact these goals.”

The lack of diversity in the DSA’s ranks and leadership has been a sore spot for the lefty organization despite its tremendous political successes in recent years — even as some of its marquee candidates have been from various races and minority ethnic and backgrounds.

Card-carrying DSA member Zohran Mamdani, who is of South Asian descent, was elected mayor last year while other successful candidates elected to Congress and the state Legislature include Latina Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier.
But other politicians have roasted the DSA for being run by mostly affluent white members, despite claiming to advocate for their minority and working class constituents.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to be the nation’s first black Speaker of the House of Representatives when Democrats take control of Congress next year, has sparred with DSA reps in his Brooklyn district.
DSA members at a primary victory party for Rep.-elect Valdez threatened Jeffries with a future primary by chanting, “You’re next!”
“It was very interesting to me, as observed by others that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd,” Jeffries told CNN of the taunts.
Meanwhile, Queens Borough President Donovan Richards said he welcomed the move by the DSA to diversify its ranks — but said the task force shouldn’t be run by white members.
“We hope the equity task force is representative of Black and brown communities,” said Richards, who is black. “We hope black and brown members will be in charge of the task force.”

The DSA has also faced accusations of hypocrisy due to embarrassing revelations in The Post that NYC-DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, a Yale University grad, was gifted a $1.5 million townhouse in Bedford-Stuyvesant by his wealthy dad — with another $1.4 million to spruce up the place.
The DSA bigwig had boasted of working-class roots and portrayed himself on social media as a hardworking labor union member.

Civil rights leader and housing activist Rev. Kevin McCall, who earlier had called for Gordillo to resign, said a task force would be a welcome first step but warned the DSA that it needs to open up the process to black and Hispanic communities in the five boroughs.

“Our campaign to hold the DSA accountable and tell the truth about their privilege is resonating with some rank-and-file members,” McCall said. “As a first test to whether their leadership will confront its own hypocrisy with meaningful action, the DSA should open the doors of their convention, invite black and brown communities into the conversation, and listen to those they claim to help.”
NYC-DSA has other ambitious goals.
Another resolution aims to elect a “socialist speaker of the City Council in 2029 to hold the mayor accountable from the left.
There are now four DSA members serving on the 51-seat City Council.

“DSA will work in coalition with other left and progressive organizations and with organized labor toward this end,” that proposed resolution said. “Recognizing that Speakers are rarely first-term members and that a socialist Speaker may not be achievable in 2029, DSA will as a fallback, support the most left-aligned viable candidate who commits to the bloc’s priorities.”

articles.headline: Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy releases in January, leaving not very long to prepare for all the crunchy cRPG choices and secret wars it'll lob your way
keyFacts: Developers Owlcat announced that the cRPG Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy will release on January 28, 2027.
The game beta version will close down on January 7, 2027, ahead of the full launch.
Players take on the role of an Inquisitor investigating heresy and commanding a warband in the Warhammer 40,000 universe.
body: Oh shit, that's not too far away. Terrifyingly, that last sentence is now a thing I can accurately write about games coming out in January 2027. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy has just been confirmed as one such game, with the cRPG's heresy investigation set to commence towards the end of the month.

January 28th, 2027, is the full Dark Heresy release date, as announced by devs Owlcat on Steam. The beta version of the game'll be closing down on January 7th to make way for the full game, so as of writing there's still some time to give that a go if you fancy.
If this is the first you've heard of Dark Heresy, here's Owlcat's synopsis of what it's all about:

Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the far future in a cRPG set in the rich Warhammer 40,000 universe. Start your service as an acolyte of the Inquisition: Investigate heresy, command a diverse warband, and shape the fate of the Calixis Sector in a story-rich experience where every decision has weight, justice is non-existent, and the line between salvation and damnation is razor-thin. Explore an in-depth depiction of the Inquisition as an organisation and the vast force it commands: its power, bureaucracy, and inner conflicts laid bare like never before.

As an Inquisitor, you have one primary goal: to protect the Imperium, whether that be from the taint of xenos, the betrayal of heretics, or the scourge of mutants, by any means necessary. Be the conduit of the Emperor’s will in a place where all hope was lost decades ago, explore the mysteries of the maddening Tyrant Star, and overcome the worst horrors thrown at you by the Noctis Aeterna.

A place where all hope was lost decades ago? You sure this is the Warhammerverse and not real life lads? I jest, but bursting into rooms and shouting 'Nobody expects the God-Emperor’s inquisition!' Monty Python-style does sound quite fun. Oisin's previously written in more depth about what Dark Heresy devs have said regarding what to expect from its investigations, if you want nitty-gritty details rather than references to sketch comedy.
If you're so inclined, Dark Heresy is wishlistable on Steam.

articles.headline: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
keyFacts: AI security researchers at Apiiro discovered that thousands of secrets are being exposed on public GitHub instances through Claude Code settings files.
The leak happens because Claude Code settings files containing sensitive information are not properly excluded at the repository level by gitignore settings.
Apiiro researchers found over 100,000 cases of local settings files uploaded to GitHub, with about 1,100 containing sensitive information like passwords and API tokens.
body: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.

Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

articles.headline: AMD users are reporting a misfiring utility is eating SSD health by 1% a month. AMD says a fix is on the way for its GPU drivers
keyFacts: Users reported that an AMD Adrenalin driver utility is causing SSD health to drop by one percent each month.
AMD representatives stated they are investigating the disk write issue and working on a resolution.
An AMD representative confirmed the bug is expected to be fixed in the upcoming Adrenalin 26.11.1 release.
body: I fear opening the Pandora's box that is my SSD's health report. I'd much rather live in ignorance until the day it inevitably fails on me. Some eagle-eyed AMD GPU users, however, have spotted their own SSD health dropping much faster than they expected, and have placed the blame squarely on an AMD Adrenalin driver utility.

Redditor Darklinkpower has flagged the issue on the r/pcmasterrace subbreddit. "I just found out that the driver eats up 1% of my SSD health every month for 16 month," says the redditor, "where[as another] user reported losing approximately 1% of their SSD health every month."

The reports come from multiple sources, including the Radeon subreddit, and Tomasz Gawroński on X, who says that Adrenalin driver utility atieclxx.exe had performed 19.5 GB of I/O writes on their machine in just 12 hours. According to Gawroński, the bug has been present since Adrenalin Edition 26.7.1 released in June of this year.
The issue doesn't appear to be present on all machines, and our own AMD GPU-using Jacob Fox hasn't been able to reproduce it. Still, the reports are numerous enough to suggest something is amiss.

In terms of an official response, representative AMD_Matt on the AMD community forums replied to a user flagging the issue last month, saying "We're looking into it with the aim to resolve it in a future driver release." Another AMD representative on Reddit, AMD_Vik, confirmed the disk write issue "should be fixed" in Adrenalin 26.11.1, although no exact release date has been given beyond its expected arrival later this month.

It seems that AMD is well aware of its misfiring utility, so hopefully the fix is on its way. After all, SSDs are bloomin' expensive at the moment, so I, along with the rest of the PC gaming community, are likely going to be eeking out the ones we've got for some time to come.

articles.headline: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
keyFacts: Thick smog shrouded New Delhi on Monday after residents set off firecrackers during Diwali celebrations, causing the air quality index to exceed 350 and reach the severe category.
The festival fireworks compounded New Delhi's seasonal air pollution crisis, which is worsened annually by winter weather, crop-residue burning, vehicle emissions, and construction dust.
Authorities have implemented measures like construction limits and court restrictions on firecrackers, but public health experts say more permanent, long-term solutions are needed.
body: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution

NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.
Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.
Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.
"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.
Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.
Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government's response so far as "knee-jerk" and "temporary."
"A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something," she said.
